title: 2025 AMA Prior Authorization Physician Survey (survey results document)

history.reason: Read in full for the distribution investigation (issue #11); this is the survey document itself, complementing the AMA articles used in PR #9

source_type: survey results document (44-question web survey, fielded December 2025, n=1,000 practicing physicians from a Medscape panel; 400 primary care / 600 specialists)
reliability: The primary document for the AMA's 2025 survey wave (released alongside the AMA's May 2026 survey coverage; exact document release date not stated in the document). Same advocacy caveat as all AMA prior-auth material; methodology (panel, screening, sample mix) is stated in the document.
findings: Phone is the most commonly used method for completing prior authorizations for medical services; only 24% of physicians report their EHR offers electronic prior authorization for prescription medications.

Determining whether authorization is even required is itself a major task: 63% (medications) and 62% (medical services) of physicians say it is difficult to determine whether a prior authorization is required, and 27% say the requirement information in their EHR is rarely or never accurate.

Appeals are rationed by capacity: only 21% of physicians always appeal an adverse decision, and among reasons for not appealing, 52% cite insufficient practice staff, resources, or time (59% cite expected futility; 49% say patient care cannot wait).

Volume and staffing context: 40 prior authorizations per physician per week, 13 hours of physician and staff time, 40% of physicians have staff working exclusively on prior authorization, and 32% report requests are often or always denied.
The document reports results by specialty mix, payer, and line of business, but publishes no breakdown by practice size or ownership.
limitations: Self-reported, advocacy-published, panel sample (Medscape) rather than a probability sample of practices.
No practice-size segmentation — the small-practice question cannot be answered from this document.
Percentages describe physicians, not practices or staff time directly.
